choices.content:
equal to, less than, or greater than \(BM+CM,\) depending upon
the position of \(M\)

question.prompt:
Let \(ABC\) be an equilateral triangle inscribed in circle \(O.\) \(M\) is a point on arc \(BC.\) Lines \(AM,\) \(BM,\) and \(CM\) are drawn. Then \(AM\) is:

[Figure 1](figures/1957_AMC_12_Q48_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
To compare \(AM\) with \(BM+CM\), we will make the sum the length of one straight segment. First suppose \(M\) lies in the interior of the arc \(BC\) not containing \(A\), as shown.

The points occur around the circle in the order \(A,B,M,C\). Opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral \(ABMC\) are supplementary, so
\[
\angle BMC=180^\circ-\angle BAC=120^\circ.
\]
Construct an equilateral triangle \(CMN\) on the side of line \(CM\) opposite \(B\). Its \(60^\circ\) angle at \(M\) adjoins \(\angle BMC\), giving
\[
\angle BMN=120^\circ+60^\circ=180^\circ.
\]
Thus \(B,M,N\) are collinear with \(M\) between \(B\) and \(N\), and
\[
BN=BM+MN=BM+CM.
\]
It remains to show that \(BN=AM\). At \(C\), ray \(CB\) lies inside \(\angle ACM\). Writing \(\theta=\angle BCM\), the equilateral triangles give
\[
\angle ACM=60^\circ+\theta=\angle BCN.
\]
Triangles \(ACM\) and \(BCN\) have \(AC=BC\), \(CM=CN\), and equal included angles at \(C\). They are congruent by SAS, so \(AM=BN\). Combining this with the segment sum proves \(AM=BM+CM\).

If \(M=B\), the equality becomes \(AB=0+BC\); if \(M=C\), it becomes \(AC=BC+0\). Both hold because \(ABC\) is equilateral. Therefore \(AM=BM+CM\) throughout the indicated arc, choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
solutions.title: Turn the sum into one straight segment
